title: Final: data, safety and dependencies
sub: The struct copy, the safety system, job chains, allocators, parallel writing and batchSize — questions, two coding tasks and practice in Unity
cards/0/q: A job accumulates a total in the field sum. After Complete() the main thread reads job.sum and sees 0. Why?
cards/0/options/0: The job received a copy of the struct, and the sum was computed in the copy. Results come back only through a container, such as NativeReference<float>
cards/0/options/1: Burst does not support float fields in jobs and silently zeroes them
cards/0/options/2: Complete() did not wait for the job to finish; you need to check IsCompleted
cards/0/options/3: The sum field must be marked [WriteOnly], then the value comes back
cards/0/explain: Schedule() copies the job struct, and Execute works on the copy. Plain fields are inputs; they never travel back. The result gets out only through a native container, because a copy of the struct points to the same memory. For a single value, use NativeReference<T>.
cards/0/wrong/1: float is the most ordinary blittable type; Burst handles it fine.
cards/0/wrong/2: Complete() does wait for the job. The issue is not timing but that the work happened in a copy.
cards/0/wrong/3: [WriteOnly] applies to containers and restricts access; it does not return field values.
cards/1/q: What is true about the safety system? Select all.
cards/1/options/0: In the Editor, two independent jobs writing to one NativeArray cause an exception when the second is scheduled
cards/1/options/1: In a player build the same checks catch the race and log an error
cards/1/options/2: [ReadOnly] lets two jobs read the same container at the same time
cards/1/options/3: A disabling attribute such as [NativeDisableParallelForRestriction] lifts the check, and guaranteeing there are no races is on you
cards/1/options/4: If the safety system stays silent in the Editor, the code certainly has no race
cards/1/explain: In the Editor the safety system knows who reads and writes each container and throws on a conflict without a dependency. In a player build those checks are unavailable, so a race there is silent data corruption. [ReadOnly] allows parallel reads. Disabling attributes switch the check off entirely: past that line the safety system sees nothing, so its silence proves no absence of races.
cards/2/q: Lay out a crowd physics frame: a chain of jobs from positions to transforms.
cards/2/items/1: Spatial hash: NativeParallelMultiHashMap.ParallelWriter buckets objects into cells
cards/2/items/2: Collisions: read your own cell and its neighbours, write contacts
cards/2/items/3: Transforms: write the new positions into each Transform
cards/2/items/4: Complete() the last JobHandle — once, when the result is needed
cards/2/explain: Each link gets the previous link’s JobHandle through dependsOn, and the whole chain runs on worker threads while the main thread does its own work. The hash is built from the new positions, and collisions read the finished hash. Complete() comes only at the end: completing the last link completes all the earlier ones.
cards/3/q: Trap: which line takes away the chain’s parallelism with the main thread?
cards/3/explain: hash.Complete() in the middle of the chain: the main thread waits for two jobs even though the next links would get the dependency through hash anyway. Delete that line — the dependency is already passed as the third argument to Schedule, and the result can be collected in LateUpdate through handle.
cards/4/task: Radar: CullJob (an IJobParallelFor with a NativeList<int>.ParallelWriter) selects the visible points, SumJob (an IJob) adds up their weights into NativeReference<float> total. In Update, schedule cull over positions.Length (second argument 64), then sum depending on cull, and store sum’s handle in the field handle. Wake the worker threads. Complete() and reading total.Value go in LateUpdate.
cards/4/checks/1/label: SumJob is scheduled with a dependency, and its JobHandle is stored in the field handle
cards/4/checks/3/label: There is no Complete() in Update
cards/4/checks/4/label: LateUpdate calls Complete(), then reads total.Value
cards/4/explain: All buffers are Persistent and reused; Clear() resets the list length without reallocating. SumJob reads visible only after the cull — the dependency guarantees it, not a Complete(). Completing the last handle in LateUpdate completes the whole chain, and until then the main thread is free.
cards/5/q: In code review: the positions buffer is created every frame with new NativeArray(..., Allocator.Persistent) and freed in LateUpdate. It works. What do you say?
cards/5/options/0: The buffer is needed every frame — allocate it as Persistent once in Awake, reuse it, and free it in OnDestroy after Complete(). Persistent every frame is the slowest allocation with no lifetime checks
cards/5/options/1: Switch to Allocator.Temp — it is the fastest and needs no Dispose
cards/5/options/2: It is all fine: Persistent is more reliable than TempJob, leave it
cards/5/options/3: Drop the Dispose: Persistent frees itself when you exit Play Mode
cards/5/explain: You pick an allocator by lifetime. Data needed every frame is long-lived: one Persistent allocation and one free. A one-off buffer into a job is TempJob; scratch data inside a job is Temp.
cards/5/wrong/1: Main-thread Temp cannot be passed into a job: in the Editor Schedule() throws an exception.
cards/5/wrong/2: It works, but it pays for the most expensive allocation every frame, and nobody catches a forgotten Dispose after 4 frames here.
cards/5/wrong/3: Persistent lives until Dispose: without it you get a leak, which leak detection will report.
cards/6/q: Match each container with how it writes from a parallel job
cards/6/pairs/1/1: Enqueue, grows in blocks by itself
cards/6/pairs/2/1: TryAdd, false on a repeated key
cards/6/pairs/3/1: A buffer per index, a stable order
cards/7/q: An IJobFor over 300 agents, ScheduleParallel(agents.Length, 512, default). In the Timeline a single thread computes the whole job. Why, and what do you do?
cards/7/options/0: 300 is less than 512 — that makes one batch, and one thread runs a batch. The work is heavy, so batchSize 1 and a check in the Timeline
cards/7/options/1: ScheduleParallel always runs on one thread; you need Schedule
cards/7/options/2: There are too few worker threads: on a machine with more cores the job will spread out by itself
cards/7/options/3: Call Complete() earlier so the main thread helps
cards/7/explain: A batch is indivisible, and the batch count is length / batchSize rounded up — one here. For heavy, uneven work batchSize is kept small, down to 1, and then you check whether the tail is gone.
cards/7/wrong/1: The other way round: ScheduleParallel is the parallel variant, while IJobFor’s Schedule runs everything on one worker thread.
cards/7/wrong/2: However many cores there are, there is one batch — and one thread will run it.
cards/7/wrong/3: Completing earlier only makes the main thread wait; there is still one batch.
cards/8/task: ScheduleHeat schedules two jobs and waits right away. Fix it: BlurJob reads tmp, which SampleJob writes — schedule it with a dependency on the first job (the third argument to Schedule). Remove every Complete(): the method returns a JobHandle that will be completed later. Free tmp without waiting: call tmp.Dispose with BlurJob's handle and return the handle Dispose gives back.
cards/8/checks/0/label: BlurJob is scheduled with a dependency on SampleJob
cards/8/checks/2/label: tmp is freed with Dispose(JobHandle) after BlurJob
cards/8/checks/3/label: There is no tmp.Dispose() without an argument
cards/8/checks/4/label: The method returns the JobHandle that tmp.Dispose(...) returned
cards/8/explain: The original has two bugs at once: without a dependency BlurJob reads tmp while SampleJob writes it (an exception at scheduling in the Editor, a race in a build), and Complete() plus an immediate Dispose() kill the parallelism. With the dependency and Dispose(JobHandle), the whole “sample → blur → free” chain runs on worker threads, and the caller collects it with a single Complete().
cards/9/q: Trap. A colleague on Collections 2.x writes: var map = new NativeHashMap<int, int>(n, Allocator.TempJob); job.map = map.AsParallelWriter(); What happens?
cards/9/options/0: It does not compile: in Collections 2.x NativeHashMap has no AsParallelWriter. For parallel writing use NativeParallelHashMap
cards/9/options/1: It works, but the key order is nondeterministic
cards/9/options/3: It compiles, but the safety system throws when the job is scheduled
cards/9/explain: In Collections 2.1 the old map with parallel writing became NativeParallelHashMap, and NativeHashMap is now single-threaded with no parallel writer. Code from older tutorials does not build on 2.x — a common lead-in to “which version did you work with?”.
cards/9/wrong/1: It never gets as far as ordering: NativeHashMap in 2.x has no AsParallelWriter method.
cards/9/wrong/2: Burst has nothing to do with it: the method is not in the API.
cards/9/wrong/3: The error comes earlier — at compile time.
cards/10/q: You are asked to explain out loud: “Why does a race throw an exception in the Editor but not in a build?” Put the answer in order.
cards/10/items/0: In the Editor every native container has a safety system handle: Unity knows which jobs read and write it
cards/10/items/1: Scheduling a job that conflicts with an unfinished one, without a dependency, throws
cards/10/items/2: These checks exist only in the Editor: in a player build they are unavailable, not merely switched off
cards/10/items/3: So in a build the same race is silent data corruption or a crash, not an error in the log
cards/10/items/4: Takeaway: I catch races in the Editor, and in a build correctness comes from dependencies, not from checks
cards/10/explain: Mechanism → rule → cost: who keeps track (the safety system handle), when it fires (a conflict without a dependency), why a build is silent (there are no checks) and what that means for your work.
cards/11/body:
A 45–60 minute task. Unity 6 with the Burst, Collections and Mathematics packages. A radar over 50,000 points.

  1. Make a MonoBehaviour with Persistent buffers: 50,000 float3 positions (random in a 500 m cube), weights, a NativeList<int> visible with capacity equal to the point count, and a NativeReference<float>. Allocate them in Awake, free them in OnDestroy after Complete().
  2. Every frame: MoveJob (IJobFor, ScheduleParallel) moves the points, CullJob with a ParallelWriter selects points within a radius of the camera, SumJob (IJob) adds up the weights. Chain them through dependsOn, call JobHandle.ScheduleBatchedJobs() after scheduling, and Complete() in LateUpdate.
  3. Write a second version of the filter with two passes — counts → ScanJob → WriteJob — and a switch between the two.
  4. Run MoveJob and CullJob with batchSize 1, 8, 64, 512 and 8192.

What to measure.

  • Profiler → Timeline: the jobs run on worker threads during the other Update calls; check for WaitForJobGroupID in LateUpdate; see how the picture changes with batchSize — a tail at 8192, longer times at 1.
  • With the camera still, compare the first indices in visible across two frames: with ParallelWriter the order changes, with the two-pass version it does not.
  • Temporarily remove the Dispose() from OnDestroy, set Leak Detection Level to EnabledWithStackTrace and wait for a domain unload (for example, a script recompile): the console shows a leak report with the allocation stack. Put the Dispose() back.
  • Temporarily drop SumJob’s dependency: in the Editor you should get a safety system exception at scheduling.

You are done when the main thread barely waits in LateUpdate; the console shows no leaks and no exceptions; the weight sums of the two filter versions match; and you can name the batchSize after which the time stops dropping, and explain why.
